Work is for the Shudra, agriculture for the Vaishya, the rod-policy for the king; celibacy, austerity, mantras and truth among the twice-born.
mahabharata:12:92.5	The kshatriya among them who knows how to remove faults of character, as cleansing garments, is father and Prajapati.
mahabharata:12:92.6	The Krita, Treta, Dvapara and Kali ages, bull of the Bharatas—of all the conduct of kings, the king alone is called the age.
mahabharata:12:92.7	The four classes, the Vedas and the four stages of life are all confused when a king is careless.
mahabharata:12:92.8	The king alone is the maker of beings and the king alone their destroyer; he who is righteous-souled is the maker and the unrighteous-souled the destroyer.
mahabharata:12:92.9	The king's wives, sons, relatives and friends all together grieve when the king is careless.
mahabharata:12:92.11	Strength was created by the Creator for the weak, Mandhata; that great being, the weak, in which everything is established, is so called.
mahabharata:12:92.12	Whatever being there is, it serves; beings and those who follow them; when a king is unrighteous, all sink, lord of the earth.
mahabharata:12:92.13	The eye of the weak and of a sage, like a venomous serpent, I consider unbearable; do not approach the weak.
mahabharata:12:92.14	Know the weak, dear one, always as the slighted; let the eyes of the weak not burn you with your kin.
mahabharata:12:92.15	In the family of one burned by the weak nothing sprouts; it is burned to the root; do not approach the weak.
mahabharata:12:92.16	The weak is better than the strong; the strength that is very strong, of one burned by the weak, leaves nothing remaining.
mahabharata:12:92.17	Slighted, struck, crying out, if he finds no protector, the superhuman-made rod slays the king.
mahabharata:12:92.18	Do not rest on strength, dear one, nor harass the weak; let the eyes of the weak not burn you like fire a house.
mahabharata:12:92.19	The tears of the falsely accused as they weep fall and kill sons and cattle of those who falsely rule them.
mahabharata:12:92.20	If not on himself, then on sons, if not on sons then on grandsons and sons' sons; a sin committed does not bear fruit at once, like a cow.
mahabharata:12:92.21	Where a weak man being slain finds no protector, there a great fate-made dreadful rod falls.
mahabharata:12:92.22	When officials seek alms from the country like Brahmanas, such men kill the king by the fault of begging again and again.
mahabharata:12:92.23	When many king's men in the king's domain act unjustly, that is a great sin of the king.
mahabharata:12:92.24	When officials take things out of desire or under the sway of wealth from those piteously begging, that is a great slaughter by the king.
mahabharata:12:92.25	A great tree is born and grows, and beings rest on it; when the tree is cut or burned, those who rested on it become homeless.
mahabharata:12:92.26	When in the kingdom they practise the highest dharma, or speak of refinement or the king's qualities, and by them adharma is practised through confusion of dharma, one should quickly give up both good and bad deeds.
mahabharata:12:92.27	Where sinners flourish and go about, there the strife of the good finds the king; when the king rules men who will perish, the king's land does not prosper, lord of the earth.
mahabharata:12:92.28	The king who honours his minister duly and employs him in counsel and war prospers; his kingdom flourishes and he enjoys the whole earth long.
mahabharata:12:92.29	Considering here well-done deeds and well-spoken speech, honouring them, the king attains unsurpassed dharma.
mahabharata:12:92.30	When he enjoys after sharing, does not scorn others, and slays the proud strong, that is called the dharma of a king.
mahabharata:12:92.31	When he protects all by speech, body and deed, and does not tolerate even his son's wrongs, that is called the dharma of a king.
mahabharata:12:92.32	When the king guards those seeking refuge like a son and does not break the boundary, that is called the dharma of a king.
mahabharata:12:92.33	When, endowed with faith, he sacrifices with sacrifices with proper fees, disregarding desire and aversion, that is called the dharma of a king.
mahabharata:12:92.34	When he wipes the tears of the wretched, helpless and aged, creating joy in men, that is called the dharma of a king.
mahabharata:12:92.35	He increases friends, draws away enemies and honours the good; that is called the dharma of a king.
mahabharata:12:92.36	He maintains truth, always gives land by right, honours guests and servants: that is called the dharma of a king.
mahabharata:12:92.37	Where both restraint and favour are established, the king gains the fruit of that in this world and the next.
mahabharata:12:92.38	Yama is the king of the righteous, Mandhata, the supreme lord; restraining, he takes life; he who does not restrain is a sinner.
mahabharata:12:92.39	When he rightly takes up priests, household priests and teachers, honouring and not slighting them, that is called the dharma of a king.
mahabharata:12:92.40	Yama restrains all beings without distinction; that is to be imitated by the king: the subjects are to be governed duly.
mahabharata:12:92.41	All kings are compared to the thousand-eyed; the dharma he sees is dharma, bull among men.
mahabharata:12:92.42	Learn with carefulness forbearance, understanding, steadfastness and mind; ever inquire into the nature of beings, good and bad.
mahabharata:12:92.43	Gathering all beings, giving and sweet speech; townsfolk and country folk are to be guarded as one's own subjects.
mahabharata:12:92.44	An unskilled king can never protect the subjects; kingship is a very great, very hard burden, dear one.
mahabharata:12:92.45	A king wise and brave, who knows the rod, can protect; it cannot be done by one without the rod, a weakling or the unwise.
mahabharata:12:92.46	You should test all minds of the handsome, those born in good families, skilled, devoted and learned, even those of ascetic hermitages.
mahabharata:12:92.47	Then you will know the supreme dharma of all beings; in your own country or another's your dharma will not perish.
mahabharata:12:92.48	Dharma, wealth and desire—dharma alone should be supreme; here and hereafter the knower of dharma prospers in happiness.
mahabharata:12:92.49	Honoured men give up wives and life; so too gathering beings, giving and sweet speech.
mahabharata:12:92.50	Carefulness and purity are greatly productive of prosperity, dear one; never be careless regarding these, Mandhata.
mahabharata:12:92.51	A king should be careful, seeing the weak points of himself and others; others should not see his weak point, and he should go after theirs.
mahabharata:12:92.52	This is the conduct of Vasava, Yama, Varuna and all royal sages; you too should follow it.
mahabharata:12:92.53	Do that, great king, the conduct served by royal sages; take quickly the divine path, bull of the Bharatas.
mahabharata:12:92.54	A king whose conduct is righteous is praised, in this world and the next, by divine sages, ancestors and Gandharvas of immeasurable splendour.
Thus addressed, Mandhata by Utathya did that without fear, and alone obtained the earth.
You too, a lord of the earth, like Mandhata, practising dharma and protecting the earth, will gain a place in heaven."

Here too they recite this ancient history, sung by the wise Vamadeva, who saw the truth of things.
mahabharata:12:93.3	A king named Vasumanas, Kausalya, strong and pure, questioned the great sage Vamadeva, who was famous:
mahabharata:12:93.4	Revered one, instruct me with words joined to dharma and wealth, by whose conduct I may not fall from my own dharma."
The ascetic Vamadeva, best of reciters, said to him, who was seated golden-hued like Yayati son of Nahusha:

Follow dharma alone; there is nothing higher than dharma; kings established in dharma conquer this earth.
mahabharata:12:93.7	The lord of the earth who regards dharma as higher than success in wealth and makes his mind truthful shines by dharma.
mahabharata:12:93.8	A king who sees unrighteousness and acts by force soon falls away, both the first and the middle.
mahabharata:12:93.9	A minister who is bad and the most sinful, destroyer of the world's dharma, is to be killed; with his retinue he soon sinks.
mahabharata:12:93.13	On these very things the conduct of the world is established; hearing them one gains fame, renown, fortune and subjects.
mahabharata:12:93.14	One so zealous for dharma, considering dharma and wealth, who begins after examining aims, surely gains greatness.
mahabharata:12:93.15	A non-giver, not very affectionate, turning the subjects by the rod, a king of rash nature soon perishes.
mahabharata:12:93.16	One with sin done by intelligence, the unwise who does not see, joined with infamy, goes to hell after death.
mahabharata:12:93.17	When there is calamity of one who honours, gives, is pure and knows savour, men wish to ruin him as if it were their own.
mahabharata:12:93.18	One who has no teacher in dharma and does not ask others, who is given to ease in gaining wealth, does not enjoy greatness for long.
mahabharata:12:93.19	One who gives primacy to teachers in dharma and himself looks to affairs, giving primacy to dharma, attains greatness long in the worlds.

The kingdom follows the king who promotes sin and has undisciplined men and soon perishes.
mahabharata:12:94.3	The livelihood by which people live of one in his natural condition, even his own people do not tolerate when he is in an uneven condition.
mahabharata:12:94.4	Where one of rash nature does something excessive, a king not marked by the scriptures soon perishes.
mahabharata:12:94.5	A kshatriya who does not follow the long-practised livelihood toward the conquered and unconquered falls from kshatriya dharma.
mahabharata:12:94.6	A king who, having taken in battle an enemy who has done his deed, does not honour him out of hatred falls from kshatriya dharma.
mahabharata:12:94.7	A king should be able, of pleasant face, and show kindness in calamity; he becomes dear to beings and does not fall from fortune.
mahabharata:12:94.8	Whoever does unpleasantness to him, to him he should do pleasantness more; he who does what is pleasant to one unpleasant soon becomes dear.
mahabharata:12:94.9	He should avoid falsehood, do what is pleasant unasked, and not abandon dharma from desire, rage or hatred.
mahabharata:12:94.10	He should not be ashamed of questions, nor utter overbearing speech, nor hurry, nor be envious; so he gathers others.
mahabharata:12:94.11	He should not rejoice too much at the pleasant, nor burn at the unpleasant, nor be bewildered in hard matters, remembering the welfare of the subjects.
mahabharata:12:94.12	The lord of the earth who ever does the pleasant for the deserving, his works succeed and fortune does not leave him.
mahabharata:12:94.13	One turned back from the hostile, following the pleasant, a king should serve the devoted; that is the conduct of the good here.
mahabharata:12:94.14	He should employ in a great task one with senses not scattered, wise, wholly devoted, pure, able and loving.
mahabharata:12:94.15	One endowed with merits so, who does not please the king and is envious of the master's aims, he should not employ in a task.
mahabharata:12:94.16	The foolish, the sensual, the greedy, the ignoble, the crafty, the one who has not passed tests, the violent, the ill-minded and the unlearned,
mahabharata:12:94.17	the abandoned, the drunk, the addicted to dice, women and hunting: the king who employs such in a great task falls from fortune.
mahabharata:12:94.18	A king who guards himself and protects those to be protected has subjects who prosper, and surely gains greatness.
mahabharata:12:94.19	He should have all kings watched by friends who are unknown; thus a king is not harmed.
mahabharata:12:94.20	Having wronged one in strength, he should not be reassured that he is far; these fall on the careless as birds of prey follow.
mahabharata:12:94.21	Firm-rooted and pure of soul, knowing his own strength, he should attack the weak, not the stronger.
mahabharata:12:94.22	Having won the earth by valour and protected the subjects by dharma, a king devoted to dharma should meet death in battle.
mahabharata:12:94.23	All this ends in death; nothing here is free of disease; therefore a king established in dharma should protect the subjects by dharma.
mahabharata:12:94.24	Protection, administration of justice, war, instruction in dharma and counsel, and happiness in due time: by these five the earth prospers.
mahabharata:12:94.25	The king, best of kings, by whom these are guarded, constantly acting here, enjoys this earth.
mahabharata:12:94.26	These cannot be watched continuously by one alone; establishing trusted men in them, a king enjoys the earth long.
mahabharata:12:94.27	People love a giver, a sharer, gentle and pure, one who does not abandon his men.
mahabharata:12:94.28	One who, knowing the supreme good, accepts that knowledge, setting aside his own opinion, is followed by the world.
mahabharata:12:94.29	One who does not tolerate the words of an asker for wealth out of hostility, and listens to the unpleasant with an absent mind, ...
mahabharata:12:94.30	One who does not utterly understand the intellect of non-rustic conduct falls from kshatriya dharma, toward the conquered and unconquered.
mahabharata:12:94.31	One who abandons chief ministers and favours lesser ones falls into calamity and finds no foothold, afflicted.
mahabharata:12:94.32	One who does not esteem kinsmen of good qualities out of hatred, weak of self and strong in anger, his wealth does not stay near.
mahabharata:12:94.33	One who, having subdued those endowed with merits, even though unpleasant to the heart, with kindness, stays long in fame.
mahabharata:12:94.34	He should not apply aims at the wrong time, nor burn at the unpleasant, nor rejoice too much at the pleasant, but be engaged in healthy work.
mahabharata:12:94.35	Which kings are devoted to me, which are in refuge from fear, and what are their neutral faults?"—he should ever consider.
He should never, being strong, trust in the weak; these fall like bharunda birds on the careless.
Even a master endowed with all merits and pleasant in speech is betrayed by a sinful soul; therefore he should fear men.
This secret teaching of kings was told by Yayati son of Nahusha; engaged in the conquest of men, he slew unsurpassed enemies."

He should not seek the unobtained when his root is not very firm; for no gain is prescribed for a king with a weak root.
mahabharata:12:95.3	A king whose country is prosperous, rich, whose king is dear, whose ministers are content and well fed, is firm-rooted.
mahabharata:12:95.4	A king whose warriors are well contented, comforted and well stationed conquers the earth even with a little rod.
mahabharata:12:95.5	A king whose townsfolk and country folk are devoted and well honoured, rich and with grain, is firm-rooted.
mahabharata:12:95.6	When he deems his might and time greater than another's, then a wise man may seek enemy land and wealth.
mahabharata:12:95.7	The domain of one hasty in enjoyments, merciless, and of one compassionate to beings, increases when he guards himself.
mahabharata:12:95.8	One who acts falsely among his own who act rightly cuts himself, as one cuts a forest with an axe.
mahabharata:12:95.9	Enemies of a king are not diminished even when he kills them constantly; one who knows how to restrain anger has no enemy.
Told so by Vamadeva, the king did all that. Doing likewise, you too will surely conquer both worlds.
A king, with or without allies, coming to the kingdom, should say: I am your king, and I shall always protect you.
What lawful tax will you give me? Will you accept me?" If they choose him who has come, it would be well.
If they, though not kshatriyas, oppose in any way, they are to be restrained by all means, lord of men, as those standing in wrong deeds.
Another, deeming the kshatriya powerless, takes up a weapon, thinking him incapable even of protection.
Then, grandsire, a kshatriya king who approaches a kshatriya—how should he be opposed? Tell me that.
A kshatriya should not be fought in battle unarmed or without armour; he should be told one by one, Let go and I strike."
If he comes armoured, one should be armoured; if he comes with an army, one with an army should challenge him.
If he fights with deceit, one should fight him with deceit; if he fights by dharma, one should resist him only by dharma.

One with weapon broken, horses lost, bowstring cut and vehicle destroyed should be healed in his own country or sent to his own house; even an unwounded one should be released: this is the eternal dharma.
Therefore one should fight by dharma, said Manu Svayambhuva; in the good the dharma of the good is ever, and relying on it one should not destroy it.
A kshatriya who conquers by unrighteousness, growing, kills himself by himself, a sinner living by deceit.
This is the work of the wicked: the good should conquer the wicked; death by dharma is better than victory by sin.
Adharma practised, O king, does not bear fruit at once like a cow; burning its roots and branches, it follows.
Having obtained wealth by sinful action, the sinner is delighted; growing by theft, the sinner clings to sin.
Thinking "There is no dharma," as if laughing at the pure, by lack of faith he goes to destruction.
Bound by Varuna's nooses, he thinks himself immortal, swelling like a great bellows, he grows by his own deed.
Then he is uprooted like a tree from a river bank; and then they revile him like a pot broken on a stone; therefore a king should seek victory by dharma as he wishes."

Victory joined to adharma is impermanent and does not lead to heaven; it ruins the king and the earth, bull of the Bharatas.
mahabharata:12:97.3	One with broken armour, saying I am yours", with joined palms and weapons laid down should be taken and not harmed.
One conquered by force should not be fought by the lord of the earth; he should be kept for a year; then he may become one born anew.
A maiden carried off by force should not be asked for before a year; likewise all wealth and anything else seized suddenly.
Barren wealth should not stay; let Brahmanas drink the milk; oxen may be yoked, or it should be forgiven.
A king should fight a king, so is dharma ordained; one who is not a king should never attack a king.
If a Brahmana comes between two armies that have met, wishing peace, then there should be no fighting on either side; one who crosses a Brahmana would break the eternal boundary.
If a kshatriya, so called, crosses this boundary, he is thereafter not praised and not to be admitted to assembly.
A king desiring victory should not follow a livelihood that breaks dharma and boundaries; what gain greater than victory won by dharma?
He should quickly appease beings who are suddenly overwhelmed, by conciliation and gifts of enjoyments; that is the highest policy of kings.
Those afflicted from their own kingdom by mismanagement would serve the enemies, waiting for a flood of calamity.
They would quickly give assistance to his enemies in a calamity, being everywhere disaffected, O king, wishing the king's misfortune.
An enemy should not be cut off utterly in any way; for a man cut off excessively may give up life at once.
An offender is pleased with even a little; such a person values even pure life greatly.
A king whose country is prosperous, rich, whose king is dear, whose servants and ministers are content, is firm-rooted.
Priests, household priests, teachers and others esteemed by the learned, who are worthy of honour and honoured by him—he is called a world-conqueror.
By this very conduct the best of gods obtained the earth, and kings after him wished to conquer, following Indra.
Having conquered in battle a king's city excepting the land, Pratardana ever brought the nectar of herbs.
Divodasa brought the agnihotras, the fire's remains and the oblation vessels, and was then wronged.
In kingdoms with kings Nabhaga gave fees, except from learned Brahmanas and ascetics, Bharata.
The conduct of the kings of old who knew dharma was high and low, Yudhishthira; all that pleases me.
A lord of the earth should not wish for victory through superior knowledge, nor by illusion or hypocrisy, who wishes his own prosperity."
By what deed does a king conquer the worlds? Tell me, wise bull of the Bharatas, who wish to know.

By restraining sinners and gathering the good, by sacrifices and gifts, kings become pure and spotless.
mahabharata:12:98.4	Kings, wishing victory, oppress beings; those same, having won, make the subjects flourish again.
mahabharata:12:98.5	They throw off sins by the strength of gifts, sacrifices and austerity; by favour to beings their merit increases.
mahabharata:12:98.6	As a field-weeder weeding the field at once destroys the weeds and grain and yet the grain is not lost,
mahabharata:12:98.7	so those who release weapons slay those to be slain at once; their atonement is complete, and the fostering of beings again.
mahabharata:12:98.8	He who protects beings from loss of wealth, from slaying and torment, from robbers, by giving life, the wealth-giver, happiness-giver, is a Virat.
mahabharata:12:98.9	A king who has sacrificed with all sacrifices with fees of fearlessness, having enjoyed good things here, attains Indra's world.
mahabharata:12:98.10	One who comes forth and fights when a Brahmana's need arises, raising himself as a sacrificial post, his is a sacrifice with endless fees.
mahabharata:12:98.11	Fearless, scattering enemies and receiving arrows, the gods see nothing better than this on earth.
mahabharata:12:98.12	As many weapons as split his skin in battle, so many worlds he gains, yielding all desires, imperishable.
mahabharata:12:98.13	The blood does not flow from his limbs from the wounds; by that very blood he is freed from all sins.
mahabharata:12:98.14	The sufferings he bears in the burning of wounds—there is no austerity greater than this, so the knowers of dharma know.
mahabharata:12:98.15	The cowardly, vilest of men, stay behind in battle, seeking refuge from the brave as livelihood from the rain-cloud.
mahabharata:12:98.16	If the brave one protected in peace as in fear, people would do likewise; but it is not so.
mahabharata:12:98.17	If, knowing what he has done, they always bowed to him and did right and just, but it is not so.
mahabharata:12:98.18	Among men who are equals a great difference is seen in battle at the hour of the line, when shouts rise and they rush forward.
mahabharata:12:98.19	The brave falls facing the enemy; the coward flees, taking a path that does not lead to heaven, abandoning his companions in difficulty.
The world has deeds as its heirs and is marked by connection with deeds; deeds urge here; as is proper, so are we.
Having cast him out of that kingdom, they consecrated his son Suvarchas, O king of kings, and he was glad.
And that I gave not this blazing fortune of father and grandfather to the Pandava, the great-souled and virtuous...
How was Bhurishravas, with his arm cut off, fasting in battle, struck down by you with a very cruel slaying—by a hero?
The delicate princess, deserving of comfort, Purandara, should go with us; let you permit it.
Those who are in this foul-smelling, very dreadful place—I do not know the misdeed of all those doers of merit.
